title: Certain About Clouds
pitch: A bureaucratic inspection machine looks at cloud-like blots (procedural, or painted by the visitor) and announces what they are with 99-percent-plus certainty: a lighthouse, a nomad, a parade float. Its reasoning transcript is delightfully wrong but fully deterministic, so the visitor can learn its rulebook by predicting its verdicts before it speaks, then try to build a blot that forces it to say a chosen word. The fun is the moment you can finish its sentence.
whyNow: Timeless. Confident machine verdicts are a permanent cultural joke, and this one swaps randomness for a rulebook that rewards understanding.

research.summary: Pareidolia (seeing faces or familiar shapes in random patterns, with clouds a classic trigger) is a normal perception effect and a subtype of the broader apophenia. Classic expert systems (knowledge base of rules, inference engine, explanation facility answering how and why) give the structure: a forward-chaining rulebook with a printed reasoning trace is both historically real and ideal for a learnable joke. Research on model calibration (stated confidence versus real accuracy, for example Guo et al., ICML 2017) gives the comic law: this machine's certainty is a fixed function that ignores contradicting evidence. Confidently wrong satirical chatbots exist (at least one is a custom GPT); a deterministic, learnable machine is a different experience. No claim on the page is a scientific finding beyond these background definitions.

facts.claim: Pareidolia is the tendency to perceive familiar patterns, especially faces, in random or ambiguous stimuli; clouds and textured surfaces are typical triggers, and it is described as a normal function of perception rather than a disorder.
Apophenia is the broader tendency to perceive meaningful patterns in random data; pareidolia is its visual subtype (some sources use the terms interchangeably).

A textbook expert system has a knowledge base of rules, an inference engine (forward chaining starts from known facts and applies rules) and an explanation facility that answers how and why questions.
Guo et al. (ICML 2017) report that modern neural networks are miscalibrated, so predicted confidence no longer matches how often they are correct; temperature scaling is their simple remedy.
Satirical chatbots built to give confidently wrong answers already exist, for example Fikry and the custom GPT Wrong Answers Only, so the page contrasts itself by being deterministic and learnable.

inspirations: classic rule-based expert systems and their why/how traces
satirical confidently-wrong chatbots (as a contrast, not a copy)

design.coreLoop: Each case is a 48x48 blot with six measured features (tallness, symmetry, holes, jaggedness, blob count, density). The visitor predicts the verdict by picking from a shortlist of six candidate words and a confidence band, then the machine stamps its verdict and prints a numbered reasoning trace of the rules that fired. A rule notebook lets the visitor state a hypothesis (feature, threshold, label) and see it scored against every past case. Depth comes from rule priority quirks (first high-salience rule wins, contradicting evidence is ignored, confidence rises with the number of agreeing weak rules). Later audits unlock a build-a-blot mode where the goal is to force a target word, for example the machine's word for a wandering traveller.
sophisticationHooks: Real forward-chaining engine in about 30 rules with salience and conflict resolution, plus an explanation trace that replays the firing order
Hypothesis notebook that auto-tests the visitor's own rule against all seen cases and highlights the counterexamples
Deterministic seeded blot generator plus freehand painting with pointer events, features computed live
Shareable URL hash that stores a case seed and the visitor's rule list, plus a printable certificate of certainty as a screenshot moment
design.scopeForOneDay: Built: seeded blot generator and freehand painter, feature extractor (6 features), forward-chaining engine with about 20 rules and 24 verdict words (lighthouse, nomad, jubilee float and similar), predict-then-reveal loop with a six-word shortlist, printed reasoning trace, single-condition rule notebook scored against past cases, build-a-blot target mode with 4 to 5 audits, certificate drawn on canvas, share hash for seed and rule list, light and dark, keyboard and touch, about panel. Cut: sound, accounts, online data, 30-rule base, user-written rule languages beyond the single-condition notebook, printable PDF.
risks: Rule base has to be learnable: a script-checked simple decision tree reproduces at least 90 percent of verdicts, and the build tests with fresh eyes.
Output could feel random if salience ties are unresolved; a stable tie-break order is shown in the trace.
Expert-system and calibration statements are background definitions with dated sources; the about panel lists only verified sources.
Freehand painting at 390px wide needs a large canvas and touch handling; features are computed on a 48x48 downsample so the engine stays deterministic.
The machine parodies a generic automated certainty under an invented bureau name with drawn stamps, never a real product's voice or branding.
The sentence about existing confidently wrong chatbots stays out of the page body or is shown as 'as of 2026-10-12, per directory listings'.

verification.notes: Pareidolia, expert-system and calibration background was returned by several independent results, and the chatbot-parody genre by three; none of these claims is load-bearing for play. Scope is trimmed to about 20 rules and 24 words; the open risk is whether the rulebook is learnable, which the build proves with a script.
